courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Nomenclature of an alternating supply: the sinusoidal waveform with its positive and negative half-cycles, the instantaneous value v = Vmax sin(wt), and the relations w = 2*pi*f = 2*pi/T linking angular frequency, frequency and period
Peak value and peak-to-peak value: the peak (maximum) value Vmax is the largest instantaneous value measured from zero, and the peak-to-peak value is 2*Vmax

RMS (effective) value defined as the steady direct current or voltage that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistance, giving Irms = Imax/sqrt(2) = 0.707*Imax and Vrms = Vmax/sqrt(2), with Vmax = sqrt(2)*Vrms = 1.414*Vrms

Why the factor 1/sqrt(2) appears: the mean of sin^2(wt) over a complete cycle is 1/2, so the mean square is Imax^2/2 and its root is Imax/sqrt(2); the mean of the sinusoid itself over a full cycle is zero, and the rectified half-cycle mean is (2/pi)*Imax = 0.637*Imax, giving form factor 1.11 and peak factor 1.414

Average power in an AC circuit: Pav = Irms^2 * R = Vrms^2/R = Vrms*Irms = (1/2)*Vmax*Imax for a resistor, with maximum instantaneous power Pmax = Vmax*Imax = 2*Pav, and generally Pav = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) where cos(phi) = R/Z is the power factor

Phase relationships of the passive elements with a sinusoidal supply: voltage and current in phase in a resistor; voltage leading current by 90 degrees in an inductor, with reactance X_L = 2*pi*f*L; voltage lagging current by 90 degrees in a capacitor, with reactance X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C); neither reactance dissipates average power

Series RLC circuits as second-order circuits in which the current is common to all components while the voltage drops are out of phase, so Kirchhoff's voltage law is applied vectorially: Vs = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2) and Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), with I = Vs/Z

Phase angle and circuit character: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R, so X_L > X_C gives an inductive circuit with the current lagging and X_C > X_L a capacitive circuit with the current leading; at series resonance X_L = X_C, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)), Z falls to R, the current is a maximum and the power factor is unity

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: Higher-order derivatives are derivatives of derivatives: f''= (f')', f'''= (f'')', and generally f^(n)(x) = d/dx[f^(n-1)(x)] with f^(0)(x) = f(x), n a non-negative integer

Notation for the orders: prime f', f'', f''' then bracketed f^(4), f^(5), ..., f^(n); Leibniz d^2y/dx^2, d^3y/dx^3, d^ny/dx^n; and the operator form D_x^n y, where the superscripts count differentiations and are not exponents
Why d^2y/dx^2 is not (dy/dx)^2 and f^(n)(x) is not [f(x)]^n: d^2y/dx^2 is the operator d/dx applied twice, (d/dx)(dy/dx), so the counter sits on the d and on the whole dx
The physical chain for displacement s(t): s' is velocity, s'' is acceleration, s''' is jerk and s^(4) is jounce, with speed increasing exactly when velocity and acceleration have the same sign
The sign of f'' as concavity: f'' > 0 means concave up with increasing gradient, f'' < 0 means concave down, and a point of inflection requires f'' to change sign, not merely to be zero

The second-derivative test at a stationary point: f'(a) = 0 with f''(a) > 0 gives a local minimum, with f''(a) < 0 a local maximum, and with f''(a) = 0 the test is inconclusive so the sign of f' either side must be used

Calculating higher-order derivatives by iterating the Week 5 rules, including the repeated product rule (uv)'' = u''v + 2u'v' + uv'', repeated chain rule where the inner derivative reappears once per order, and implicit second derivatives that require substituting dy/dx back in

General nth-derivative patterns: e^(ax) -> a^n e^(ax), sin x -> sin(x + n*pi/2), 1/x -> (-1)^n n! x^-(n+1), ln x -> (-1)^(n-1) (n-1)! x^-n, and a degree-n polynomial whose nth derivative is the constant a*n! and whose (n+1)th derivative is zero

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: Definition: a pseudocode is a textual representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program, or the textual representation of an algorithm, written in a form that makes it easily convertible into programming statements of any language

What it is for: writing all the main steps of an algorithm in a language very similar to English, the rule of thumb that you write the pseudocode first when you are struggling to start a program, and the technique of writing the pseudocode into the file as comments and then filling in the actual code between them

The rules that govern pseudocode: each line contains only one statement, keywords are written in capital letters, statements must be language independent and not in a particular programming language, and the body of every construct is indented

The eight constructs and their skeletons: SEQUENCE (with the verbs READ/OBTAIN/GET, PRINT/DISPLAY/SHOW, COMPUTE/CALCULATE/DETERMINE, SET/INIT, INCREMENT/BUMP, DECREMENT), FOR ... ENDFOR, WHILE ... ENDWHILE, REPEAT ... UNTIL, IF-THEN-ELSE-ENDIF, CASE ... OTHERS ... ENDCASE, CALL with and RETURNING, and EXCEPTION with WHEN inside a BEGIN ... END block

Where each loop tests its condition: FOR sets all the necessary conditions at the beginning/top, WHILE sets some condition at the top and other conditions in the body so its body may run zero times, and REPEAT-UNTIL sets its condition at the ending/bottom so its body always runs at least once; FOR i = a TO b runs b - a + 1 times because both bounds are inclusive

Algorithms versus pseudocode: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that can be expressed in any language - natural language, programming code or mathematical symbol - and is precise and well defined, while pseudocode is a high-level, informal representation of it in a combination of natural and programming language elements, not meant to be executed as the actual code

The seven steps of writing a pseudocode - problem definition, identification of main steps, header writing (name, purpose, inputs and outputs), using variables and data structures, using constructs to describe logic, using clear and concise language, and testing and refining - applied to the course's worked problem of counting passes and failures and deciding whether tuition should be increased

Advantages (no special software needed, understandable by anyone because the language is close to English, easily modified, structured concepts easily implemented) and disadvantages (no generally accepted standards so styles vary, not visual compared with flowcharts, and slower to read and understand than a flowchart)

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Aim of the experiment: investigate the charging characteristics of a capacitor and determine its capacitance and time constant

Theory of the capacitor: two conductors separated by a distance d with plate area A and a dielectric of permittivity epsilon, so C = epsilon*A/d; charge stored is Q = CV; capacitors pass AC and block DC and are used as filters in DC supplies and as energy-storage banks

Charging law: V(t) = V0 * (1 - e^(-t/tau)), where charge transfers until the p.d. between the conductors equals the p.d. across the charging device's terminals, and the current I = (V0 - V)/R falls as V rises

Time constant: tau = RC in seconds with R in ohms and C in farads; tau is the time to charge to 63.2 percent of maximum or discharge to 36.8 percent of the initial value, with about 99.3 percent reached after 5 tau, so increasing R at fixed C increases tau and the circuit charges more slowly

Apparatus and circuit: voltmeter, power supply, charging circuit (capacitor, resistor, switch key), stopwatch and wires in the Praxilabs virtual RC Circuit Charging laboratory, with the voltmeter in parallel across the capacitor

Procedure: connect the circuit, set the supply output voltage, close the switch key and record the voltmeter reading every 10 seconds until maximum voltage, taking at least 10 readings, then end the trial and download the data sheet

Data analysis and graph: plot V on the y-axis against t on the x-axis, find 63.2 percent of the maximum voltage and trace to the time axis to read tau; alternatively plot ln(V0 - V) against t for a straight line of gradient -1/tau and intercept ln V0

Calculations and errors: obtain C = tau/R and the percentage error = (theoretical - experimental)/theoretical x 100, worked for the sample trial (V0 = 1 V, R = 10 kohm, tau about 9.97 s giving C about 997 microfarads, 0.3 percent error), plus precautions and sources of error such as reaction time, voltmeter loading, dielectric leakage, component tolerance and lead resistance

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Nigeria's indigenous trade system thrived between 1500 and 1800 AD, shaped by geography and natural resources, with regions specialising in agriculture, trade or craftsmanship and exchanging what they produced for what they lacked

The Niger River was pivotal to the growth of indigenous trade, international markets drew traders from other regions, and inter-group exchange produced cultural diffusion alongside the movement of goods; the apprenticeship system passed skills and knowledge down the generations
Colonial intrusion disrupted the indigenous system, transforming Nigeria's precolonial economy into the Western capitalist economic model and altering social and political structures with it

At independence agriculture was the hub of the economy: over fifty per cent of GDP before independence and over 75% of the workforce in 1960, with Development Corporations significant in the regional political structure, and GDP growth rising from 1.89% in 1960 to 4.89% in 1965, Nigeria being tipped for the world's 20 largest economies by 1980 ahead of Malaysia

The coups and the civil war truncated economic progress, the 1970s oil boom was not saved for rainy days, agriculture was abandoned for easy oil money, and the mid-1980s crunch brought austerity measures under the Buhari regime followed by the IMF-pressured Structural Adjustment Programme

SAP further weakened the economy: the currency began a downward movement and the manufacturing base was destroyed as imported goods made local products uncompetitive on price and quality; the second oil boom of the 1990s was looted by Sani Abacha into foreign banks

The democratic era: GDP growth rose from 0.58% to 6.59% after 1999, Obasanjo secured $20 billion in debt relief and reserves above $64 billion, reserves fell to $34 billion by 2015 under Goodluck Jonathan despite oil above $100, and from 2014 US shale oil cut American purchases, India replaced the US as the major buyer, and the budget has run a deficit financed by borrowing

Causes of Nigeria's economic woes -- over-dependence on crude oil, corruption, banking insider abuse and capital-market round-tripping, poor economic policies, violence and pipeline vandalisation, and the absence of economic planning -- and the solutions proffered, from diversification and curbing corruption to electricity, industrial parks, local refining, lower cost of governance, effective tax collection and tourism

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Three written forms defined: a summary condenses a larger text to its main ideas and essential information; a letter is a written message to a specific person or group; a report is a formal document presenting information, analysis, findings and conclusions on a specific issue

The eight ordered steps of summary writing: read carefully, identify the thesis, highlight key points, condense in your own words, maintain the original structure, eliminate unnecessary details unless crucial, check coherence, review and revise
Summary-writing conventions: own words throughout, no new material, no personal opinion, no direct quotation, roughly one third or less of the original length

The nine ordered steps of letter writing: identify purpose and audience, choose the format, greeting, introduction, body in organised paragraphs, politeness and tone, closing, closing salutation, review and edit

The five key parts of the sample letter - greeting, opening sentence, statement of purpose, closing, signature - plus the convention that 'Yours sincerely' follows a named salutation and 'Yours faithfully' an impersonal one
The eleven ordered steps of report writing, from defining the purpose and gathering data through methodology, findings, conclusions and recommendations to references, appendices and final review

The standard report sections and what belongs in each: introduction (topic, purpose, scope), methodology (how data were gathered, for transparency and reliability), findings (evidence, with graphs, charts or tables), conclusions (interpretation, no new data), recommendations (actionable steps)
Worked samples traced through: a condensed summary of a passage on politics, a letter of appreciation from Hollie Holdings, and a report on global poverty section by section

checks.topic: Higher-order derivatives as concepts: what the second, third and nth derivatives mean, the prime, Leibniz d^ny/dx^n and D^n notations and why they are written that way, the physical reading as velocity, acceleration and jerk, and what the sign of f''(x) says about concavity, points of inflection and the second-derivative test

questions.q: The symbol d^2y/dx^2 is correctly read as:
options: the square of dy/dx, since the numerator and the denominator have both been squared
the operator d/dx applied twice to y, i.e. d/dx(dy/dx) - the superscripts count differentiations
the derivative of y with respect to the quantity x^2, i.e. differentiating against a squared variable
dy/dx divided once more by dx, so a further division by the increment
questions.concept: Leibniz notation as a repeated operator, not an algebraic power
questions.why: d^2y/dx^2 is (d/dx)(d/dx)y, so the 2 records that the whole operator d/dx has acted twice - hence one 2 on the d and one on the dx. Reading it as a square gives (dy/dx)^2, a genuinely different function.

questions.q: For a particle moving in a straight line with displacement s(t), s'''(t) is:
options: the acceleration, since acceleration is the third quantity after position and speed
the cube of the velocity
zero for every motion, because acceleration is constant
the jerk - the rate of change of the acceleration with respect to time
questions.concept: The order chain: displacement, velocity, acceleration, jerk
questions.why: Each derivative of displacement steps one rung up the rate-of-change ladder: s' is velocity, s'' acceleration, s''' jerk. Constant acceleration is only the special case of a quadratic s(t).

questions.q: f is a polynomial of degree 5. Which is true?
options: f^(5)(x) is a non-zero constant and f^(6)(x) = 0 for all x
f^(5)(x) = 0 for all x, since five differentiations exhaust a degree-5 polynomial
f^(5)(x) is linear in x and f^(6)(x) is a non-zero constant
no derivative of f is ever identically zero, because a polynomial can be differentiated indefinitely
questions.concept: Degree falls by exactly one per differentiation
questions.why: Degree 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0, so the fifth derivative is the constant 5! times the leading coefficient and only the sixth is identically zero.

questions.q: At a point where f'(a) = 0, finding f''(a) > 0 tells you that:
options: the curve is rising at x = a, since a positive second derivative means the function is increasing
the curve is concave up at x = a, so the stationary point is a local maximum
the curve is concave up at x = a, so the stationary point is a local minimum
x = a is a point of inflection, because a non-zero f''(a) rules out a turning point
questions.concept: The second-derivative test
questions.why: A horizontal tangent with the gradient increasing through a means f' runs negative, zero, positive: the bottom of a bowl, i.e. a local minimum.

questions.q: For a twice-differentiable f, "f''(c) = 0" means:
options: c is certainly a point of inflection
c is only a candidate: it is a point of inflection if f'' actually changes sign at c
c is certainly a stationary point of f
f is a straight line near c, since zero curvature means no bending
questions.concept: f'' = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for an inflection
questions.why: y = x^4 has y'' = 12x^2, zero at x = 0 but non-negative on both sides, so the concavity never changes and x = 0 is a minimum, not an inflection.

questions.q: A car's velocity is negative and its acceleration is positive. The car is:
options: moving backwards and speeding up, since a positive acceleration always increases speed
instantaneously at rest, since the two opposite signs cancel
moving backwards but slowing down, since velocity and acceleration have opposite signs
moving forwards, because the sign of the acceleration fixes the direction of travel
questions.concept: Speed changes with the sign of v times a, not the sign of a
questions.why: d/dt(v^2/2) = v*a, so speed falls exactly when v and a have opposite signs. Here the car travels in the negative direction with its speed decreasing.

questions.q: A company's profit satisfies P'(t) > 0 and P''(t) < 0. Then:
options: profit is falling, because the second derivative is negative
profit is rising at an ever-increasing rate
profit is exactly at its maximum value at this instant
profit is still rising, but by less and less as time goes on
questions.concept: First derivative gives direction, second gives how that rate is changing
questions.why: P' > 0 means profit is increasing; P'' < 0 means the rate of increase is itself falling, so the graph rises while bending over.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3, which pair of values is correct?
options: f''(x) = 9x^4, since the double prime is shorthand for the derivative squared
questions.concept: The prime counts differentiations; squaring is a different operation
questions.why: f'(x) = 3x^2, so f''(x) = 6x, whereas [f'(x)]^2 = (3x^2)^2 = 9x^4 - unrelated functions.

questions.q: Explain what d^2y/dx^2 instructs you to do, why the superscripts sit on the d and on the dx rather than on y and on x, and why d^2y/dx^2 and (dy/dx)^2 are different objects. Give one function where the two are visibly different.
questions.concept: Leibniz notation as a repeated operator, not an algebraic square
questions.why: d^2y/dx^2 means differentiate y with respect to x and then differentiate the result again: (d/dx)(dy/dx). Because it is the operator d/dx that repeats, the counter goes on the d in the numerator and on the whole dx in the denominator; d^2y/d^2x would wrongly attach it to the variable, and no d may be cancelled because dy/dx is a single symbol for a limit, not a ratio. (dy/dx)^2 is instead one derivative multiplied by itself. For y = x^3: d^2y/dx^2 = 6x while (dy/dx)^2 = (3x^2)^2 = 9x^4. A dimensional check settles it: with y in metres and x in seconds, d^2y/dx^2 is in m/s^2 but (dy/dx)^2 is in m^2/s^2.

questions.q: A student says "f''(x) > 0 means the function is increasing." State precisely what f''(x) > 0 does mean, and give a function that is decreasing on an interval while f'' > 0 throughout that interval.
questions.concept: Concavity versus increase: f' and f'' carry independent information
questions.why: f''(x) > 0 means the gradient is increasing, i.e. the curve is concave up and lies above its tangents; it says nothing about whether f itself rises, since a gradient can increase from -5 to -1 and stay negative. Example: f(x) = e^(-x) has f'(x) = -e^(-x) < 0 everywhere (decreasing) yet f''(x) = e^(-x) > 0 everywhere (concave up). Simpler still, f(x) = x^2 on x < 0 has f' = 2x < 0 and f'' = 2 > 0. All four sign combinations of f' and f'' occur.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of what each derivative measures, why acceleration is the second derivative of displacement, and why "negative acceleration" does not by itself mean "slowing down". State the correct test for speeding up.
questions.concept: Each order is the rate of change of the order below; speed depends on v times a
questions.why: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt = d/dt(ds/dt) = d^2s/dt^2 - second because it is one rate of change applied to another. Negative acceleration means the velocity is decreasing (more negative or less positive), which is not the same as the speed |v| falling. Since d/dt(v^2/2) = v*a, speed increases when v and a have the same sign and decreases when they differ. A particle with v = -4 m/s and a = -2 m/s^2 is speeding up backwards despite the negative acceleration.

questions.q: Explain why a polynomial of degree n must have f^(n)(x) equal to a non-zero constant and f^(n+1)(x) = 0, and say what that constant is for f(x) = a x^n. What does this say about how many orders of derivative a polynomial model can carry information in?
questions.concept: Differentiation lowers polynomial degree by exactly one
questions.why: Differentiating a x^k gives k a x^(k-1): the degree falls by exactly 1 and the leading coefficient stays non-zero while k >= 1. From degree n, after n differentiations the degree is 0 (a constant) and after n+1 it is the zero function, which then stays zero. The successive leading coefficients are an, an(n-1), an(n-1)(n-2), ..., so f^(n)(x) = a*n! - for f(x) = 3x^5, f^(5) = 3*120 = 360. Consequence: a degree-n polynomial carries real information in only n orders, so a quadratic displacement model has constant acceleration and zero jerk built in and cannot describe changing acceleration.

checks.topic: A.C. nomenclature as concepts: what peak, peak-to-peak, rectified mean and rms actually mean, why rms is defined by equal heating power and where the 1/sqrt(2) comes from, the phase behaviour of R, L and C under a sinusoidal supply, reactance, and why the impedance of a series RLC circuit adds in quadrature rather than arithmetically

questions.q: The rms value of an alternating current is defined as:
options: the average of the instantaneous values of the current taken over one complete cycle
the greatest instantaneous value the current reaches during a cycle, measured from zero
the value of the steady direct current that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistance
the square root of the peak value, which is where the figure 0.707 comes from
questions.concept: RMS defined by equivalent heating power
questions.why: An alternating current of rms value 5 A heats a given resistor at exactly the rate a steady 5 A DC would, which is why rms is also called the effective value and why the definition works for any waveform. Option a is the full-cycle mean, which for a sinusoid is zero and would predict no heating at all; option b defines the peak value; option d invents an arithmetic origin, since 0.707 is 1/sqrt(2) obtained from the mean of the square.

questions.q: The factor 1/sqrt(2) that relates Irms to Imax for a sinusoid arises because:
options: the mean of sin^2(wt) over a complete cycle is 1/2, and the rms value is the square root of that mean square
the mean of sin(wt) over a half-cycle is 2/pi, and sqrt(2) is what converts that into a peak value
a sinusoid is negative for half of every cycle, so half of the peak value must be discarded
average power is proportional to the current rather than to its square, so averaging the sinusoid itself supplies the factor
questions.concept: rms is the root of the mean of the square
questions.why: i^2 = Imax^2 sin^2(wt) and sin^2(wt) = (1/2)(1 - cos 2wt), whose cosine term averages to zero over a cycle, so the mean square is Imax^2/2 and its root is Imax/sqrt(2). Option b is the route to the rectified mean 0.637*Imax; option c wrongly discards the negative half-cycle, which heats just as much because i^2 is positive there; option d is the very misconception the definition exists to defeat, since power goes as i^2 and not as i.

questions.q: In a pure inductor carrying a sinusoidal current:
options: the voltage across it lags the current by 90 degrees, because an inductor always opposes a change in current
the voltage across it leads the current by 90 degrees, because the induced emf responds to the rate of change of the current
voltage and current stay in phase, but the voltage amplitude is reduced by the factor wL
the voltage leads the current by an angle between 0 and 90 degrees whose size depends on wL
questions.concept: Phase in an inductor: voltage leads current by 90 degrees (ELI)
questions.why: v_L = L(di/dt), so with i = Imax sin(wt) the voltage is wL*Imax cos(wt), a quarter of a cycle ahead. Option a states a correct physical fact but draws the opposite phase conclusion, the standard L/C swap; option c treats X_L as a resistance, which would mean zero phase shift and energy dissipation; option d confuses a single element with a combination, since an intermediate angle needs R and a pure inductor always gives exactly 90 degrees.

questions.q: The impedance of a series RLC circuit is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) rather than R + X_L + X_C because:
options: X_L and X_C are inherently negative quantities, so a square root is needed to return a positive Z
the current is different in each of the three components, so their oppositions cannot simply be summed
Kirchhoff's voltage law does not hold in an alternating circuit, so an alternative rule has to be used
the three voltage drops do not reach their maxima at the same instant (V_L is 90 degrees ahead of V_R and V_C is 90 degrees behind it), so they must be added as vectors
questions.concept: Impedance adds in quadrature because the drops are out of phase
questions.why: Only quantities that peak together may be added arithmetically; V_L and V_C are 180 degrees apart and partly cancel, leaving sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2), which divided by the common current gives Z. Option a is false, since both reactances are positive and only their difference carries a sign; option b confuses series with parallel, as in series the current is common and the voltages differ; option c is the opposite of the truth, because KVL holds exactly but as a vector sum.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is driven at a frequency for which X_C > X_L. Then:
options: the circuit is inductive, the current lags the supply voltage, and phi is positive
the circuit is at resonance, since the two reactances are partly cancelling
the circuit is capacitive, the current leads the supply voltage, and phi is negative
the current leads the supply voltage by exactly 90 degrees, since the capacitor is the dominant element
questions.concept: The sign of the net reactance fixes the circuit's character
questions.why: X = X_L - X_C is negative, so tan(phi) = X/R is negative and phi is negative: the current leads and the circuit is capacitive. Option a reverses the identification, the commonest error in the topic; option b confuses partial cancellation with the exact equality X_L = X_C that defines resonance; option d forgets R, since phi = arctan(X/R) reaches 90 degrees only when R = 0.

questions.q: Averaged over a complete cycle, the power delivered to a pure inductor is:
options: Irms^2 * X_L, since X_L is measured in ohms and plays the same role for the inductor that R plays for the resistor
(1/2)*Imax*Vmax, exactly as it would be for a resistor of resistance X_L
zero only at the resonant frequency, where X_L is cancelled by X_C
zero, because the energy stored in the magnetic field during one quarter-cycle is returned to the source during the next
questions.concept: A pure reactance stores energy rather than dissipating it
questions.why: Instantaneous power is positive for half of each cycle and equally negative for the other half, so the average is zero; equivalently Pav = VI cos(phi) with phi = 90 degrees. Option a is the reactance-as-resistance error, since I^2*X_L is reactive volt-amperes and not watts; option b applies the resistor result, which already assumes v and i are in phase; option c attaches an irrelevant condition, as the average power in a pure inductor is zero at every frequency and resonance is a property of a combination.

questions.q: The mean value of a sinusoidal current over a complete cycle is zero, yet a moving-iron ammeter in the circuit reads a definite non-zero value. This is because:
options: the meter responds only to the positive half-cycles and displays their peak value
the meter's deflection follows the mean square of the current, and its scale is calibrated to display the rms value
the meter averages the current over a half-cycle, giving 0.637*Imax, and that is what rms means
the meter measures the peak-to-peak value and halves it
questions.concept: An AC meter must respond to the square of the current
questions.why: A moving-iron or thermal instrument deflects with the square of the current, so it responds to the non-zero mean square, and its scale is marked with the square root of that, the rms value; a moving-coil meter, linear in i, would read essentially zero. Option a would display the peak; option c is the rms versus rectified-mean confusion, the two differing by the form factor 1.11; option d is the peak-to-peak confusion, since half of Ipp is the peak, not the rms.

questions.q: In a series RLC circuit under a sinusoidal supply, the quantity that is the same for R, L and C is:
options: the current, both its rms value and its phase, while the three voltage drops differ in phase
the voltage drop, because components in series all sit across the same supply
the phase of the voltage drop, because all three drops are produced by one and the same source
the average power, because the same current passes through all three components
questions.concept: In a series circuit the current is common and is the phase reference
questions.why: One conducting path means one current, identical in magnitude and phase everywhere, which is why the current is taken as the phase reference and every drop measured relative to it. Option b is the parallel property; option c is the core misconception the phasor method corrects, since each element imposes its own 0, +90 or -90 degree relationship; option d confuses same current with same power, because P = I^2*R depends on the resistance and L and C dissipate nothing.

questions.q: Explain why the effective value of an alternating current is defined through equal heating rather than by averaging the waveform. Show where the factor 1/sqrt(2) comes from for a sinusoid, and say why the rectified mean (0.637*Imax) is not used as the standard quoted value.
questions.concept: RMS defined by equal heating, because power depends on the square of the current
questions.why: Heating in a resistance is i^2*R. Since i^2 is positive in both half-cycles it has a genuine non-zero average, whereas i itself averages to exactly zero over a full cycle, so an average current would predict no heating and could not be used to rate a supply, a fuse or a cable. The effective (rms) value is therefore defined as the steady DC that would dissipate the same average power in the same resistance. For a sinusoid i = Imax sin(wt): i^2 = Imax^2 sin^2(wt) = Imax^2 * (1/2)(1 - cos 2wt); the cosine term has zero mean over a cycle, so the mean square is Imax^2/2 and Irms = Imax/sqrt(2) = 0.707*Imax. The rectified mean 0.637*Imax is a real quantity, the half-cycle average that a rectifier meter's movement actually senses, but it is not the value that predicts power: it is smaller than the rms by the form factor 1.11, so quoting it would under-state the heating by about 19 percent (0.637^2/0.707^2 = 0.81). It is also related to the rms by a different factor for every waveform, whereas rms means the same thing, equal heating, for all of them.

questions.q: Take the current as reference and explain, from v_L = L(di/dt) and i_C = C(dv_C/dt), why the voltage leads the current by 90 degrees in an inductor but lags it by 90 degrees in a capacitor. State how X_L and X_C each depend on frequency, and what each element does at f -> 0 and at f -> infinity.
questions.concept: The 90 degree phase shifts come from differentiation; frequency dependence follows
questions.why: Take i = Imax sin(wt). Inductor: v_L = L(di/dt) = wL*Imax cos(wt) = wL*Imax sin(wt + 90 degrees), so the voltage is a quarter-cycle ahead and its amplitude is wL*Imax, giving X_L = wL = 2*pi*f*L. Physically the inductor's voltage is largest when the current is changing fastest, which is as the current passes through zero, not at its peak. Capacitor: here the current is the derivative, i = C(dv_C/dt), so if v_C = Vmax sin(wt) then i = wC*Vmax cos(wt): the current is a quarter-cycle ahead, i.e. the voltage lags by 90 degrees, with X_C = 1/(wC) = 1/(2*pi*f*C). (ELI the ICE man.) X_L is proportional to f, because faster changes mean a bigger back-emf; X_C is proportional to 1/f, because at high frequency the plates never have time to charge up. At f -> 0 (DC) an inductor is a short circuit (X_L -> 0) and a capacitor an open circuit (X_C -> infinity); at f -> infinity they exchange roles, the inductor blocking and the capacitor passing.

questions.q: In a series RLC circuit the measured drops are V_R = 60 V, V_L = 130 V and V_C = 50 V, yet the supply is only 100 V. Explain why this does not violate Kirchhoff's voltage law, why V_L alone can exceed the supply voltage, and what rule replaces simple addition.
questions.concept: KVL in an AC circuit is a vector sum
questions.why: KVL still holds instant by instant: at every moment v_s = v_R + v_L + v_C. What fails is adding the amplitudes, because the three drops reach their maxima at different times. With the common current as reference, V_R is in phase with it, V_L is 90 degrees ahead and V_C is 90 degrees behind, so V_L and V_C are 180 degrees apart and directly oppose one another. The rule that replaces simple addition is Vs = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2). Here V_L - V_C = 130 - 50 = 80 V, so Vs = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = sqrt(3600 + 6400) = sqrt(10000) = 100 V, exactly the supply. V_L alone can exceed the supply because at the instant the inductor's voltage peaks, the capacitor's is at its own opposite peak and the resistor's is passing through zero, so the sum at that instant is still only 100 V; the arithmetic sum 240 V corresponds to no instant that ever occurs. This is why a series circuit near resonance can develop component voltages several times the supply, which is a real hazard rather than a paradox.

questions.q: Explain what series resonance is, what happens to Z, I, phi and the power factor there, and why the statement 'the reactances cancel, so no current flows' is exactly backwards. Say also how you would tell, from a measurement of the phase angle alone, whether the supply frequency is above or below f0.
questions.concept: Series resonance: cancellation of reactance gives minimum impedance and maximum current
questions.why: Resonance is the frequency f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) at which X_L = X_C. The net reactance is then zero, so Z = sqrt(R^2 + 0) = R, its minimum value; I = V/R is therefore its maximum; tan(phi) = 0/R = 0 so phi = 0, current and supply voltage in phase; and the power factor cos(phi) = R/Z = 1, so the circuit absorbs the full VI as real power and behaves as pure resistance. The claim that no current flows inverts the mechanism: cancellation removes opposition, it does not insert a break. What cancels is the pair of voltages V_L and V_C, equal in size, opposite in direction, vector sum zero, and each of them individually may be many times the supply voltage by a factor Q = X_L/R. Nothing is disconnected; the loop is more open to current than at any other frequency. From the phase angle alone: if the current lags (phi > 0) the circuit is inductive, X_L > X_C, and the frequency is above f0; if the current leads (phi < 0) it is capacitive and the frequency is below f0; phi = 0 means you are exactly at f0.

checks.topic: Pseudocode concepts: what a pseudocode is and what it is for, the rules that govern it, the eight constructs and where each one tests its condition, the seven steps of writing one, its stated advantages and disadvantages, and how it relates to an algorithm and to a flowchart

questions.q: Last week's deck defined a flowchart as 'a graphical representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program'. How does this week's deck define a pseudocode?
options: As a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, which may be expressed in natural language, programming code or mathematical symbols
As a simplified programming language whose statements a compiler converts directly into a working program
As a textual representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program, or the textual representation of an algorithm
As a set of comments written into a source file to describe code that has already been written
questions.concept: the definition of a pseudocode, and the word that separates it from a flowchart
questions.why: The two definitions are the same sentence with 'textual' in place of 'graphical', which is exactly what the Pseudocodes I mid-lesson question tests ('A pseudocode is a graphical representation...' -> No). Option a is the definition of an ALGORITHM, and the giveaway is 'mathematical symbols', since pseudocode by definition uses natural and programming language elements. Option b is the 'pseudocode is nearly code' error: it is written in a form easily convertible into programming statements, which is not the same as being convertible by a compiler, and it is not meant to be executed as the actual code. Option d inverts the comments-first technique: the pseudocode becomes the comments, but it is written BEFORE the program, not as a description of code that already exists.

questions.q: A student's pseudocode contains the single line 'System.out.println(total);'. One rule is broken. Which, and why does that rule exist?
options: The one-statement-per-line rule, because printing is really two tasks - fetching total and displaying it - and each task must sit on its own line
The language-independence rule: pseudocode statements must not be written in a particular programming language, because anyone should be able to read them and convert them into any language
The capital-letters rule, because println is the output keyword on this line and keywords must be written in capitals so they stand out from other words
No rule is broken: the line holds one statement, it is understandable, and it would convert into working code without any change at all
questions.concept: language independence, and the two properties it protects
questions.why: The line is Java. Pseudocode statements are required to be language independent, not in a particular programming language, for two reasons the course states elsewhere: anyone can understand pseudocode since the language is close to English, and it is written in a form that makes it easily convertible into programming statements - any language's statements. A Java line is readable only by Java programmers and is already committed to Java, so it does neither job; 'PRINT total' or 'DISPLAY total' is the pseudocode. Option a misapplies a real rule: one statement per line means one task per line, and displaying a value is one task. Option c also misapplies a real rule: capitals are for pseudocode keywords, and println is not one - capitalising it gives SYSTEM.OUT.PRINTLN, which is still Java. Option d is the reading of the rules as style advice, when 'it converts to code without any change' is precisely the fault.

questions.q: One loop must keep reading results while a condition set at its top still holds, with further conditions inside the body deciding what happens on each pass. A second must run a number of times that is fixed entirely before it is entered. Which two constructs, in the course's own terms?
options: The first is FOR, since all its conditions are set at the beginning/top; the second is WHILE, since it runs a desired number of times
The first is REPEAT-UNTIL and the second is FOR, since only REPEAT-UNTIL is allowed to carry conditions in the body of its statements
The first is WHILE, which sets some condition at the beginning/top and other conditions in the body; the second is FOR, which sets all the necessary conditions at the beginning/top
Both are WHILE loops, because FOR is only a shorthand for a WHILE whose counter has been written out in full at the top
questions.concept: where each loop construct sets its conditions
questions.why: The course distinguishes the loops by the placement of the conditions: FOR executes statements a desired number of times based on setting ALL the necessary conditions at the beginning/top; WHILE does so based on setting SOME condition at the beginning/top and OTHER conditions in the body of the statements; REPEAT-UNTIL sets some condition at the ending/bottom and other conditions in the body. 'Some at the top, others in the body' is WHILE; 'all at the top' is FOR. Option a swaps the two, which is what a vague memory that both test at the top produces. Option b picks REPEAT-UNTIL on the strength of 'conditions in the body', which WHILE has too - the discriminator is the top/bottom placement. Option d is a true-sounding fact from programming practice that answers a different question: the course names them as separate constructs on exactly this distinction.

questions.q: In the CASE skeleton, what is OTHERS for, and what is CASE said to be?
options: OTHERS lists the variables that the expression does not test; CASE is a more generalised form of the FOR loop
OTHERS is the default sequence, run when none of the listed conditions holds; CASE is a more generalised form of the conditional statement that IF-THEN-ELSE also provides
OTHERS is the handler for values the expression cannot take; CASE is the construct out of which EXCEPTION and WHEN are built
OTHERS repeats the whole CASE for any conditions still left over; CASE is a more generalised form of REPEAT-UNTIL
questions.concept: CASE as the generalised conditional, OTHERS as its default branch
questions.why: The course introduces CASE as also using conditional statements to change the normal flow of operation of an algorithm, but represented in a more generalised form - so its neighbour is IF-THEN-ELSE, not a loop. In the skeleton, condition 1 to condition n are the alternatives and 'OTHERS: default sequence' catches everything that matched none of them, which is what stops the construct doing nothing at all. Options a and d both attach CASE to a loop, the first reading 'generalised' as 'repeated for each condition' and the second making the same error with the other loop. Option c is the near-miss worth knowing: OTHERS handles a value the expression DID take that you did not list, whereas an exception handler deals with an event that occurs while the program runs - nothing in CASE is about failure.

questions.q: In 'CALL SquareRoot with orbitHeight RETURNING norminalOrbit', what do 'with' and 'RETURNING' each name?
options: 'with' names the routine that is called, and 'RETURNING' names the routine control comes back to when it finishes
'with' names the data type of the argument supplied, and 'RETURNING' names the data type of the result produced
'with' names the class in which the object is defined, and 'RETURNING' names the object that the call creates
'with' names the argument passed into the routine, and 'RETURNING' names the variable that receives the value handed back
questions.concept: reading a CALL - arguments in, result out
questions.why: The course's four examples make the pattern plain: CALL AvgAge with studentAges (argument only), CALL Swap with CurrentItem and TargetItem (two arguments), CALL getBalance RETURNING aBalance (result only), and CALL SquareRoot with orbitHeight RETURNING norminalOrbit (both). The name straight after CALL is the routine; 'with' introduces what is passed IN; RETURNING names the variable that receives what comes OUT. Option a misreads 'with' as naming the routine, which leaves SquareRoot unexplained, and treats RETURNING as a return of CONTROL rather than of a VALUE - control always resumes at the line after the CALL, so nothing would need naming. Option b invents data-type declarations, which belong to the 'using variables and data structures' step. Option c stretches the course's remark that CALL can be used for defining class objects over the whole line.

questions.q: Both CASE and EXCEPTION/WHEN pick one set of statements out of several. What distinguishes them?
options: Nothing structural: EXCEPTION/WHEN is simply CASE written for errors, and either may be used wherever the other one is
CASE may only test numeric expressions whereas WHEN may test any expression at all, which is why exceptions were given their own keyword

CASE chooses among expected values of one expression as part of the normal flow; WHEN clauses sit in the EXCEPTION part of a BEGIN...END block and run only when an unexpected or unwanted event occurs as the program runs
CASE is evaluated once before its block runs, while WHEN is re-evaluated after every statement in the block, which is what makes exception handling the slower of the two
questions.concept: selection among expected values vs handling an unexpected event
questions.why: CASE is part of the plan: you know the expression, you list its possible values, and one branch is taken every time the construct is reached. EXCEPTION/WHEN is the opposite arrangement - the statements between BEGIN and EXCEPTION are the ones meant to run, and the WHEN clauses run only when unexpected or unwanted events take place while the program is running, which the course names as exception handling. On a run where nothing goes wrong, no WHEN clause is entered at all, which no CASE can say of itself. Option a is the tempting summary 'EXCEPTION is CASE for errors', right about the shape and wrong about the trigger. Option b invents a restriction on CASE that the skeleton 'CASE expression OF' does not carry. Option d invents an execution model and reasons about speed, a question pseudocode cannot ask, since it is not executed.

questions.q: The course lists as a disadvantage that pseudocode 'takes a longer time to read and understand' than a flowchart, even though it is written in near-English. What is the mechanism behind that?
options: Pseudocode is always longer than the flowchart of the same algorithm, because each symbol expands into several lines of text that must all be read

A flowchart shows its structure at a glance in shapes and arrows; a pseudocode reader must rebuild the control flow line by line, and must first decode the writer's own style, since no accepted standards exist
Pseudocode borrows its keywords from several programming languages at once, so a reader has to know all of those languages before following any of it
Pseudocode cannot show repetition directly, so a reader has to reconstruct every loop by hand from the statements that are being repeated
questions.concept: why a textual notation costs the reader more than a graphical one
questions.why: The course's contrast is that flowcharts are visual and easily understandable while pseudocodes are not visual, and the reading-time complaint follows from it. In a chart the control flow is drawn: a loop is an arrow you can see going back, a branch is a fork you can see splitting. In pseudocode the same structure is only implied by keywords and indentation, so the reader must simulate the flow mentally. The other stated disadvantage compounds it: since there are no generally accepted standards, anyone can write pseudocode in their own way, so the writer's conventions must be worked out before the logic can be read. Option a confuses length with difficulty and is not reliably true. Option c invents a mixed-language claim that the language-independence rule forbids. Option d is false - repetition is exactly what FOR, WHILE and REPEAT-UNTIL are for.

questions.q: Which statement about algorithms and pseudocode is correct on the course's account?
options: An algorithm may be written in any notation or language while pseudocode is written in a combination of natural and programming language elements, and the algorithm is the precise, well-defined one
Pseudocode may be written in any notation or language while an algorithm must be written in a combination of natural and programming language elements, and the pseudocode is the precise one
An algorithm is a representation of a pseudocode, produced once the pseudocode has been coded in a specific programming language and tested
An algorithm and a pseudocode are two names for one thing, since both are step-by-step procedures and neither of them is executed by a machine
questions.concept: algorithm vs pseudocode - the four contrasts the course draws
questions.why: The course states them in a row: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem and can be expressed in any language - natural language, programming code or mathematical symbol; pseudocode is a high-level representation of an algorithm using a combination of natural and programming language elements, without following any specific language's syntax strictly; algorithms are usually represented as pseudocode during early software development stages, before being coded; and algorithms have precise and well-defined procedures while pseudocode is more high level and informal. Option b is the mid-lesson question's own distractor, the two terms reversed, and it also reverses the precision claim, so remembering only 'one of them is the precise one' does not rescue you. Option c reverses the direction of representation and the order of work. Option d collapses a real distinction: both are unexecuted, but the algorithm is the method and the pseudocode is one way of writing it down.

questions.q: The course recommends writing the pseudocode into a file AS COMMENTS, then filling in the actual code between those comments. Explain what problem this solves, why the course describes it as 'writing the comments for our program before writing the program', and what specifically would go wrong with the technique if the pseudocode had been written in one language's syntax.
questions.concept: pseudocode as the scaffolding of the source file
questions.why: The problem it solves is the one the course names in its rule of thumb: if you want to develop a new computer program and you are struggling with how to start the development, write a pseudocode first. The difficulty at the start is not the syntax but deciding what the steps are and in what order; writing them as comments lets you settle the whole sequence - inputs, loop, branches, outputs - while nothing in the file has to compile. Once the sequence is right, each comment is a specification for the lines beneath it, and the job shrinks from 'write a program' to a series of small local translations. Because the pseudocode was written before any code and stays in the file, we are essentially writing the comments for our program before writing the program: the commentary is not a later gloss but the design that produced the code, which is also why the comments genuinely describe what the code does. If the pseudocode had been written in one language's syntax, three things break. It stops being a design, since you have committed to that language's constructs, types and library calls before deciding whether they suit the problem. The comments become useless as comments, restating the code below them line for line instead of saying what it is for. And it fails the language-independence rule and the reason behind it: it is no longer easily convertible into the statements of ANY language, and it can no longer be read by anyone who does not know the one you chose.

questions.q: State the rules that govern the writing of a pseudocode and, for EACH one, name the specific ambiguity or failure it prevents - not what the rule says, but what a reader would be unable to work out if the rule were ignored.
questions.concept: each rule removes one ambiguity from a notation with no grammar
questions.why: ONE STATEMENT PER LINE. Pseudocode gives the computer a list of tasks to implement in a sequential manner, so the line is what carries the order. Ignore it - 'SET total TO 0; READ n; SET total TO total + n' - and the reader can no longer tell how many tasks there are, cannot cite a step by position, and cannot see whether a step was left out; worse, once several tasks share a line, indentation applies to the group rather than the task, so it stops saying which construct they belong to. KEYWORDS IN CAPITAL LETTERS. Capitals are what differentiate keywords from other words. Without them, structure cannot be told from prose: does 'if the student passed' begin an IF construct or merely describe one, and is 'set total' an instruction or a variable named settotal? Since pseudocode is deliberately close to English, the capitals are the only marker that a word is doing structural work. LANGUAGE INDEPENDENCE. Without it the pseudocode is readable only by those who know the language it leaked from, and it is no longer convertible into any language - so both properties the course claims, that anyone can understand it and that it is easily convertible into programming statements, fail at once. INDENTATION OF EACH CONSTRUCT'S BODY. This is what says how far a loop or a branch extends. Without it a reader cannot tell whether a statement after an IF belongs to the THEN part or follows the whole construct, nor whether a counter is incremented inside the loop or once after it - and the deck's own solution shows the damage, with 'add one to student counter' left outside a WHILE that therefore never advances. (The rules slide is cut off after three rules while the week's Summary sheet says four should be followed; indentation is the fourth, and every worked example in the deck obeys it.)

questions.q: List the seven steps of writing a pseudocode in order. Then explain precisely what separates PROBLEM DEFINITION from IDENTIFICATION OF MAIN STEPS, and what separates USING CONSTRUCTS TO DESCRIBE LOGIC from USING CLEAR AND CONCISE LANGUAGE, since in each pair the second step looks like more of the first.
questions.concept: the seven steps, and the two pairs that are easily collapsed
questions.why: In order: problem definition; identification of main steps; header writing; using variables and data structures; using constructs to describe logic; using clear and concise language; testing and refining. PROBLEM DEFINITION VS MAIN STEPS. Problem definition is about the problem and is written entirely in terms of inputs, process, outputs and requirements - for the tuition example, the input is the number of students and their results, the process is accepting each result and determining pass or fail, the output is the number of passes, the number of failures and the tuition decision. Nothing in it says how anything will be done or in what order; it states what a correct solution would have to take in and produce. Identification of main steps is about the SOLUTION: it breaks the problem into its integral parts and puts them in sequence - initialise the storage, set up the counters, accept a result and classify it, increment the relevant counter, display the outputs. The test that separates them: change your mind about how to solve the problem and the main steps change, while the problem definition does not. Doing the second before the first produces solutions to the wrong problem. CONSTRUCTS VS CLEAR LANGUAGE. The constructs step decides the control structure - that a WHILE will iterate over the results and an IF-THEN-ELSE will pick which counter to increment - and it is right or wrong: choose an IF where a loop was needed and the algorithm fails. The clear-language step decides the wording inside that structure, and it is about ambiguity, not correctness: 'FOR each index of string / IF string(index) is equal to hash THEN' and 'FOR i = 0 to 20 / IF string[i] = #' describe the same logic, and the course prefers the first because the second imports one language's indexing syntax. So the fifth step can leave the algorithm wrong and the sixth can only leave it unclear - but unclear is enough to fail the requirement that the constructs describe the steps without ambiguity.

questions.q: The course claims that pseudocode needs no special software, that anyone can understand it, and that it is easily modified; and it complains that there are no generally accepted standards, and that pseudocode is not visual. Explain which of the advantages and which of the disadvantages are two sides of one single property, name that property, and say what this implies about when you would choose a flowchart over pseudocode.
questions.concept: the advantages and disadvantages follow from two properties: no fixed notation, and no picture
questions.why: PROPERTY ONE: IT HAS NO FIXED SYNTAX. From this come the advantages that no special software is needed - it can be written with any text editor - that it can easily be modified, and that anyone can understand it, since the words are near-English rather than a defined grammar; and from the very same fact comes the disadvantage that since there are no generally accepted standards for writing pseudocodes, anyone can write pseudocode in their own way, leading to various styles and possible complications, especially if the pseudocode is not well written. These are one property seen from two sides: the freedom that lets you write anything is the freedom that stops a reader relying on anything. It is also why the course states rules at all - they are a voluntary standard imposed on a notation that has none, which is why breaking them costs more here than in a real language, where a compiler would object. PROPERTY TWO: IT IS TEXT, NOT A PICTURE. From this comes the rest: compared to flowcharts, which are visual and easily understandable, pseudocodes are not visual, and it takes a longer time to read and understand them - while the same property is what makes them easy to edit, since inserting a line shifts the rest down by itself, where inserting a box into a flowchart may force a redraw. IMPLICATION. Use a flowchart when the audience must grasp the shape of the logic quickly, when the structure is branching or looping enough that seeing it matters, or when non-programmers have to follow it. Use pseudocode when the design will change repeatedly, when it must be handed to programmers to convert into a specific language, or when it is to live inside the source file as its comments - and then follow the rules strictly, because they are the only standard it has.

checks.topic: Higher-order derivative problems: computing second, third and fourth derivatives of polynomials, products, quotients and composites, building the general nth-derivative formula for e^(ax), sin(ax), 1/(ax+b) and 1/x, taking implicit second derivatives, and running displacement to velocity to acceleration on a motion problem

questions.q: If y = 4x^5 - 3x^4 + 2x - 9, then d^3y/dx^3 =
questions.concept: Repeated differentiation of a polynomial; constants die at the first step
questions.why: y' = 20x^4 - 12x^3 + 2, y'' = 80x^3 - 36x^2, y''' = 240x^2 - 72x. The +2 has already become 0 in y''.

questions.concept: Product rule applied again at the second order, with the chain factor each time

questions.q: If y = e^(3x), then d^ny/dx^n =
questions.concept: nth derivative of e^(ax)
questions.why: Each differentiation reproduces e^(3x) and leaves one more factor of 3: y' = 3e^(3x), y'' = 9e^(3x), so y^(n) = 3^n e^(3x).

questions.q: The fourth derivative of y = sin 2x is:
options: sin 2x
16 cos 2x
-16 sin 2x
16 sin 2x
questions.concept: Trig derivatives cycle with period 4 while the chain factor multiplies up
questions.why: y' = 2cos 2x, y'' = -4 sin 2x, y''' = -8 cos 2x, y^(4) = 16 sin 2x = 2^4 sin 2x; the signs run +, -, -, +.

questions.q: If y = 1/x, then y^(4) =
questions.concept: nth derivative of x^-1: alternating sign, factorial coefficient, exponent n+1

questions.q: For the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25, d^2y/dx^2 =
options: -x/y
questions.concept: Implicit second derivative: substitute dy/dx back, then use the original equation

questions.q: A particle moves so that s = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t (metres, t >= 0 seconds). Its acceleration at the second instant at which it is at rest is:
questions.concept: At rest means v = 0, not a = 0
questions.why: v = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t - 1)(t - 2), so rest occurs at t = 1 and t = 2; a = 12t - 18, and a(2) = 6 m/s^2.

questions.q: d^2/dx^2 [x^3 ln x] =
options: 6x ln x
6x ln x + 3x
6x ln x + 5x
6x ln x + 2x
questions.concept: Both terms of the first derivative must be differentiated
questions.why: y' = 3x^2 ln x + x^2; y'' = [6x ln x + 3x] + 2x = 6x ln x + 5x.

questions.q: Find the general nth derivative of y = 1/(3x + 1), and say separately where the sign (-1)^n, the factorial n! and the power 3^n each come from. State y''' explicitly as a check.
questions.concept: General nth derivative of a negative power with an inner linear function
questions.why: y = (3x + 1)^-1, so y' = -3(3x + 1)^-2, y'' = 18(3x + 1)^-3 and y''' = -162(3x + 1)^-4. In general y^(n) = (-1)^n * n! * 3^n * (3x + 1)^-(n+1). The sign (-1)^n comes from the exponent being negative, so each differentiation brings down a negative number; the factorial n! comes from the magnitudes 1, 2, 3, ... of those numbers multiplying up as the exponent falls; the 3^n comes from the chain rule, which supplies the inner derivative 3 exactly once per differentiation. Check n = 3: (-1)^3 * 6 * 27 = -162, matching the direct computation.

questions.q: For y = x^2 e^(-x), find d^2y/dx^2. Then explain why the formula (uv)'' = u''v + uv'' is wrong, state the correct expansion, and show numerically at x = 1 how far the wrong formula misses by.
questions.concept: Second derivative of a product: the cross term 2u'v'
questions.why: y' = 2x e^(-x) - x^2 e^(-x) = e^(-x)(2x - x^2); y'' = -e^(-x)(2x - x^2) + e^(-x)(2 - 2x) = e^(-x)(x^2 - 4x + 2). The false formula fails because (uv)' = u'v + uv' is itself a sum of two products, each needing the product rule again: (uv)'' = (u''v + u'v') + (u'v' + uv'') = u''v + 2u'v' + uv''. Here u''v = 2e^(-x), 2u'v' = -4x e^(-x), uv'' = x^2 e^(-x), summing to e^(-x)(x^2 - 4x + 2). The false formula gives e^(-x)(x^2 + 2); at x = 1 the correct value is -e^-1 = -0.368 while the false one gives 3e^-1 = +1.104, wrong even in sign and missing by 4e^-1.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3, find the stationary points and classify them using the second derivative. Explain exactly what goes wrong at x = 0, what you do instead, and locate all points of inflection.
questions.concept: Second-derivative test and its inconclusive case
questions.why: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3), so the stationary points are x = 0 and x = 3. f''(x) = 12x^2 - 24x = 12x(x - 2). f''(3) = 36 > 0, so (3, -27) is a local minimum. At x = 0, f''(0) = 0 and the test gives no information, since a zero second derivative is consistent with a maximum, a minimum or an inflection. Fall back on the sign of f' = 4x^2(x - 3): negative for x < 0 and negative for 0 < x < 3, so the gradient does not change sign and x = 0 is a stationary point of inflection. Inflections occur where f'' changes sign, at x = 0 (plus to minus) and x = 2 (minus to plus), giving (0, 0) and (2, -16).

questions.q: For the curve xy = 12, find d^2y/dx^2 twice over: once by implicit differentiation and once by making y the subject. Show the two agree, and explain why the implicit route obliges you to substitute dy/dx back in before you can finish.
questions.concept: Implicit second derivatives must be reduced to x and y alone
questions.why: Implicitly: differentiating xy = 12 by the product rule gives y + x y' = 0, so y' = -y/x. Differentiating again: y' + (y' + x y'') = 0, i.e. 2y' + x y'' = 0, so y'' = -2y'/x. This still contains y', which is a function of x and not a constant, so y' = -y/x must be substituted back: y'' = 2y/x^2. Explicitly: y = 12x^-1, y' = -12x^-2, y'' = 24x^-3 = 24/x^3. The two agree, since 2(12/x)/x^2 = 24/x^3. The general rule is that d^2y/dx^2 must be expressed in x and y alone; an answer still containing dy/dx is unfinished.

checks.topic: Numerical A.C. work: converting between peak and rms values of current and voltage, substituting into X_L = 2*pi*f*L and X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C) with milli- and micro- prefixes, computing the impedance, current, component voltages and phase angle of a series RLC circuit, finding the resonant frequency, and calculating average, apparent and maximum power

questions.q: A mains socket is rated 220 V. The maximum instantaneous voltage it delivers is:
questions.concept: Quoted supply voltages are rms; Vmax = sqrt(2)*Vrms
questions.why: Vmax = 220 x 1.414 = 311 V. Option a divides by sqrt(2) instead of multiplying, which would make the peak smaller than the effective value, impossible for any waveform; option c is the peak-to-peak value 2*Vmax = 622 V, the crest-to-trough swing rather than the peak from zero; option d assumes peak and rms are the same number.

questions.q: An AC generator of maximum voltage 24.0 V and frequency 60.0 Hz is connected across a resistor R = 265 ohm. The rms current in the circuit is:
options: 128 mA
questions.concept: Apply the sqrt(2) conversion exactly once
questions.why: Vrms = 24.0/1.414 = 16.97 V, so Irms = 16.97/265 = 0.0640 A = 64.0 mA (equally, Imax = 24.0/265 = 90.6 mA then divided by sqrt(2)). Option a is Imax, the peak current, with the conversion never applied; option b divides the peak by 2 instead of by sqrt(2); option c multiplies by sqrt(2) instead of dividing, applying the conversion in the wrong direction.

questions.q: For that same circuit (Vmax = 24.0 V, 60.0 Hz, R = 265 ohm), the average power dissipated in the resistor is:
questions.concept: Average power uses rms values throughout
questions.why: Pav = Vrms*Irms = (16.97)(0.0640) = 1.09 W, confirmed by Irms^2*R = 1.087 W and by Vrms^2/R = 288.0/265 = 1.087 W. Option b is Pmax = Vmax*Imax = 2.17 W, the peak instantaneous power, which is exactly 2*Pav; option c mixes the two families as Vmax x Irms = 1.54 W, a quantity with no meaning; option d halves the correct average a second time, as though the 1/2 in (1/2)Vmax*Imax applied on top of the rms conversion.

questions.q: A coil of inductance 40 mH is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance is:
options: 2.00 ohm
12.6 ohm
questions.concept: X_L = 2*pi*f*L, with L in henries
questions.why: 40 mH = 0.040 H, so X_L = 2*pi*(50)(0.040) = 12.6 ohm. Option a uses f in place of w = 2*pi*f, giving 2.00 ohm, a factor 6.28 too small; option b leaves L in millihenries, a thousand times too big; option d takes the reciprocal, applying the capacitor formula to an inductor.

questions.q: A 25 microfarad capacitor is connected to the same 50 Hz supply. Its reactance is:
options: 800 ohm
127 ohm
questions.concept: X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C), with C in farads
questions.why: 2*pi*f*C = 314.16 x 25 x 10^-6 = 7.854 x 10^-3, so X_C = 127 ohm. Option a drops the 2*pi, giving 1/(50 x 25 x 10^-6) = 800 ohm; option b is the intermediate product 2*pi*f*C, the formula used without inverting it; option c leaves C in microfarads, a million times too small. A sanity check catches all three: tens of microfarads at mains frequency is worth of order a hundred ohms, never milliohms or megohms.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 12 ohm, X_L = 20 ohm and X_C = 4 ohm, driven at 120 V rms. The impedance of the circuit is:
options: 36 ohm
28 ohm
26.8 ohm
20 ohm
questions.concept: Impedance adds in quadrature, with the reactances subtracting
questions.why: X = X_L - X_C = 16 ohm, so Z = sqrt(12^2 + 16^2) = sqrt(400) = 20 ohm. Option a adds all three arithmetically, ignoring phase entirely; option b gets the net reactance right but then adds it to R arithmetically, 12 + 16 = 28; option c adds the reactances instead of subtracting them, sqrt(12^2 + 24^2) = 26.8 ohm, forgetting that V_L and V_C are in direct opposition.

questions.q: For that same circuit (R = 12 ohm, X_L = 20 ohm, X_C = 4 ohm), the phase relationship between current and supply voltage is:
options: the current leads the voltage by 53.1 degrees
the current lags the voltage by 36.9 degrees
the current lags the voltage by 53.1 degrees
the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees
questions.concept: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R, and a positive net reactance means a lagging current
questions.why: tan(phi) = 16/12 = 1.333 so phi = 53.1 degrees, and since X_L > X_C the circuit is inductive and the current lags. Option a has the right magnitude with the character reversed, which is the capacitive case; option b inverts the ratio, arctan(12/16) = 36.9 degrees, measuring the angle from the reactance axis instead of from the voltage; option d ignores R, which is what would make the angle a full 90 degrees.

questions.q: For that same circuit at 120 V rms (R = 12 ohm, X_L = 20 ohm, X_C = 4 ohm), the average power drawn from the supply is:
questions.concept: Pav = VI cos(phi) with cos(phi) = R/Z, equivalently I^2*R
questions.why: I = 120/20 = 6.00 A and cos(phi) = 12/20 = 0.600, so P = (120)(6.00)(0.600) = 432 W, confirmed by I^2*R = 36.0 x 12 = 432 W. Option b is the apparent power VI = 720 VA, the power factor omitted, i.e. the circuit treated as DC; option c squares the power factor, 720 x 0.36 = 259 W; option d uses the net reactance in place of the resistance, I^2*X = 576 W, but reactance carries no average power at all.

questions.q: An AC generator of maximum voltage 170 V and frequency 60.0 Hz supplies a 25.0 ohm resistor. Find Vrms, Imax, Irms, the average power and the maximum instantaneous power, and show explicitly that Pmax = 2*Pav. State which of your answers depend on the 60.0 Hz and why.
questions.concept: Peak-to-rms conversion in a resistive AC circuit, and the factor of two between average and peak power
questions.why: Vrms = Vmax/sqrt(2) = 170/1.4142 = 120 V. Imax = Vmax/R = 170/25.0 = 6.80 A. Irms = Imax/sqrt(2) = 4.81 A (equally Vrms/R = 120/25.0 = 4.81 A; the conversion may be done before or after dividing by R, but only once). Average power: Pav = Vrms*Irms = (120)(4.81) = 578 W, cross-checked by Irms^2*R = 578 W and exactly by Vmax^2/(2R) = 28900/50.0 = 578 W. Maximum instantaneous power: p(t) = i^2*R peaks when i = Imax, so Pmax = Imax^2*R = (6.80)^2(25.0) = 1156 W, which is also Vmax*Imax = (170)(6.80); and 2*Pav = 2(578) = 1156 W. The reason is that p(t) = Vmax*Imax*sin^2(wt) oscillates between 0 and Vmax*Imax while sin^2 averages to 1/2, the same 1/2 that produced the sqrt(2). None of these answers depends on the 60.0 Hz: in a purely resistive circuit there is no reactance, so Z = R at every frequency, and f would enter only through X_L = 2*pi*f*L or X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C). The frequency fixes only how often the power peaks, 120 times a second, not its average or peak value.

questions.q: A series circuit of R = 40 ohm, L = 0.20 H and C = 30 microfarad is connected to a 200 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Find X_L, X_C, Z, the current, all three component voltages and the phase angle (say whether the current leads or lags), then verify the supply voltage by vector addition and the average power by two independent routes.
questions.concept: The complete series RLC calculation, checked two ways
questions.why: w = 2*pi*(50) = 314.16 rad/s. X_L = wL = (314.16)(0.20) = 62.8 ohm. X_C = 1/(wC) = 1/[(314.16)(30 x 10^-6)] = 1/(9.425 x 10^-3) = 106.1 ohm. Net X = 62.8 - 106.1 = -43.3 ohm, negative, so the circuit is capacitive. Z = sqrt(40^2 + 43.3^2) = sqrt(1600 + 1872) = sqrt(3472) = 58.9 ohm. I = 200/58.9 = 3.39 A, common to all three components. Component voltages: V_R = (3.39)(40) = 136 V; V_L = (3.39)(62.8) = 213 V; V_C = (3.39)(106.1) = 360 V. Vector check: sqrt(136^2 + (213 - 360)^2) = sqrt(18500 + 21600) = sqrt(40100) = 200 V, the supply, while the arithmetic sum 709 V is meaningless; note V_C alone is nearly twice the supply, which is legitimate because V_L opposes it directly. Phase: tan(phi) = -43.3/40 = -1.082, so phi = -47.2 degrees and the current leads the supply voltage by 47.2 degrees, as a capacitive circuit must. Average power route 1: cos(phi) = R/Z = 40/58.9 = 0.679, so P = VI cos(phi) = (200)(3.39)(0.679) = 461 W. Route 2: P = I^2*R = (3.39)^2(40) = 461 W. All the power is in R. For reference f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(0.20 x 30 x 10^-6)) = 65.0 Hz, and since 50 Hz is below f0 the circuit must indeed be capacitive, an independent confirmation of the sign of phi.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 20 ohm, L = 0.32 H and C = 20 microfarad across a 60 V rms supply of variable frequency. Find the resonant frequency, and the current, impedance, power factor and average power at resonance. Compare the current with its value at 50 Hz, and find the voltage across the inductor at resonance, commenting on its size relative to the supply.
questions.concept: Series resonance: minimum impedance, maximum current, and component overvoltage
questions.why: f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)): LC = (0.32)(20 x 10^-6) = 6.4 x 10^-6, sqrt(LC) = 2.530 x 10^-3, so f0 = 1/(2*pi x 2.530 x 10^-3) = 1/0.015895 = 62.9 Hz. At resonance w0 = 2*pi(62.9) = 395.3 rad/s, X_L = (395.3)(0.32) = 126.5 ohm and X_C = 1/[(395.3)(20 x 10^-6)] = 126.5 ohm, equal, so the net reactance is zero: Z = R = 20.0 ohm (its minimum), I = 60/20.0 = 3.00 A (its maximum), phi = 0, power factor = 1, and P = VI = 180 W = I^2*R = (9.00)(20.0). At 50 Hz instead: X_L = (314.16)(0.32) = 100.5 ohm, X_C = 1/[(314.16)(20 x 10^-6)] = 159.2 ohm, X = -58.6 ohm, Z = sqrt(400 + 3437) = 61.9 ohm, so I = 60/61.9 = 0.969 A, under a third of the resonant current, and the circuit is capacitive because 50 Hz lies below f0. Voltage across L at resonance: V_L = I*X_L = (3.00)(126.5) = 380 V, more than six times the 60 V supply; V_C is the identical 380 V, exactly opposite, so their vector sum is zero and KVL is satisfied by V_R = (3.00)(20.0) = 60 V alone. The multiplying factor is Q = X_L/R = 6.3. This is the practical hazard of a lightly damped series circuit at resonance: components rated for the supply voltage can be destroyed by the internal voltages.

questions.q: For R = 15 ohm, L = 50 mH, C = 100 microfarad on a 240 V rms, 50 Hz supply, a student reports X_L = 2.5 ohm, X_C = 200 ohm, Z = 217.5 ohm and I = 1.10 A. Identify each error, name it, and give the correct values of X_L, X_C, Z, I and the average power.
questions.concept: Three separable substitution errors: f used for w, twice, then arithmetic addition of impedances
questions.why: Error 1, the 2*pi omitted in X_L: the student wrote X_L = fL = (50)(0.050) = 2.5 ohm, but X_L = 2*pi*f*L = (314.16)(0.050) = 15.7 ohm, a factor 6.28 larger. Error 2, the 2*pi omitted in X_C: the student wrote X_C = 1/(fC) = 1/[(50)(100 x 10^-6)] = 200 ohm, but X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C) = 1/[(314.16)(100 x 10^-6)] = 1/0.031416 = 31.8 ohm, where the same 6.28 makes the answer smaller because the 2*pi sits in the denominator; the prefixes themselves were converted correctly, so the sole fault is f for w. Error 3, impedances added arithmetically: the student wrote Z = R + X_L + X_C = 217.5 ohm, but impedance adds in quadrature and the reactances subtract, X = 15.7 - 31.8 = -16.1 ohm, so Z = sqrt(15^2 + 16.1^2) = sqrt(485) = 22.0 ohm. Correct results: X_L = 15.7 ohm, X_C = 31.8 ohm, Z = 22.0 ohm, I = 240/22.0 = 10.9 A (not 1.10 A, the wrongly inflated Z having throttled the current by a factor of ten), phi = arctan(-16.1/15) = -47.1 degrees with the current leading, so the circuit is capacitive. Average power = I^2*R = (118.8)(15) = 1780 W, confirmed by VI cos(phi) = (240)(10.9)(0.681) = 1780 W. An order-of-magnitude check would have caught the whole thing: with only 15 ohm of resistance on a 240 V supply the current cannot be about 1 A unless the reactances are enormous, and 50 mH at mains frequency is worth only tens of ohms.

checks.topic: Applied pseudocode: tracing a fragment line by line to what it prints, finding the bug in a fragment and naming the rule or condition it breaks, choosing the fragment that implements a stated task, and the off-by-one and loop-condition traps in FOR, WHILE and REPEAT-UNTIL

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. What is printed?
SET total TO 0
SET i TO 1
WHILE i <= 4
    SET total TO total + i
    SET i TO i + 1
ENDWHILE
PRINT total
questions.concept: tracing a pre-tested counting loop, and the inclusive <= bound
questions.why: i = 1: total = 1, i = 2. i = 2: total = 3, i = 3. i = 3: total = 6, i = 4. i = 4: total = 10, i = 5. Now 5 <= 4 is false, so the loop ends and 10 is printed, the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. Option a (6) is the off-by-one from reading 'i <= 4' as 'i < 4', which drops the last pass and always loses exactly the largest term. Option c (15) comes from letting the pass with i = 5 run, that is, from testing after the body instead of before it. Option d (5) is the final value of i, printed by a student who traced correctly and then read the wrong variable - i and total end the loop holding very different things.

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. Exactly what appears on the screen?
SET n TO 10
REPEAT
    PRINT n
    SET n TO n - 3
UNTIL n < 0
options: 10, 7, 4, 1 and then the loop stops
10, 7, 4, 1, -2 and then the loop stops
7, 4, 1 and then the loop stops
Nothing at all, because n < 0 is false when the loop is reached
questions.concept: a post-tested loop prints before it tests, and UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true
questions.why: Pass 1 prints 10, then n = 7; 7 < 0 is false, so round again. Pass 2 prints 7, n = 4. Pass 3 prints 4, n = 1. Pass 4 prints 1, n = -2; now -2 < 0 is true and the loop stops. Four lines. Option b adds -2, which assumes another PRINT before the final test - but the decrement is the LAST statement of the body, so the value that finally satisfies the condition is never printed. Option c prints after decrementing, reading the two body lines in the wrong order. Option d is the important one: it reads UNTIL n < 0 as though it were WHILE n < 0 and, finding the condition false at the start, concludes the body is skipped. Both halves are wrong - REPEAT-UNTIL tests at the ending/bottom, so the body always runs at least once, and it stops when the condition turns true rather than running while it is true.

questions.q: Which fragment reads the marks of five students, counts how many scored 50 OR MORE, and prints that count?
options: SET count TO 0; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { READ mark; IF mark > 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
FOR i = 1 TO 5 { SET count TO 0; READ mark; IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
SET count TO 0; READ mark; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
SET count TO 0; FOR i = 1 TO 5 { READ mark; IF mark >= 50 THEN SET count TO count + 1 ENDIF } ENDFOR; PRINT count
questions.concept: where the accumulator is initialised, where the read happens, and which comparison '50 or more' names
questions.why: Option d initialises count once before the loop, reads a fresh mark on each of the five passes, tests mark >= 50, and prints after the loop. Each of the others breaks exactly one of those. Option a tests mark > 50, so a student scoring exactly 50 is not counted - '50 or more' is >=, and the boundary value is the only input that separates the two fragments, which is why it is the one to test on. Option b moves SET count TO 0 INSIDE the loop, so the counter is wiped at the start of every pass and the printed value can only be 0 or 1; the plausible-looking output is what makes this bug survive. Option c reads a single mark before the loop and never reads again, so the same mark is tested five times and the answer is either 0 or 5.

questions.q:
Trace this fragment. What is printed?
SET s TO 0
FOR k = 2 TO 8
    SET s TO s + k
ENDFOR
PRINT s
questions.concept: FOR bounds are inclusive at both ends
